title: Inelastic Kinetic Decoupling in WIMP Leptogenesis: A Minimal $Z_4$ Model
comment: 28 pages, 6 figures
summary: We study a minimal $Z_4$-symmetric extension of the Standard Model in which a singlet Dirac fermion $χ$ constitutes dark matter, whose annihilations generate a lepton asymmetry through WIMP leptogenesis. Kinetic equilibrium is maintained mainly by the inelastic conversion $χL\leftrightarrow\barχΨ$. Compared with the near elastic regime, a sizable mass gap suppresses the conversion rate more rapidly as the Universe cools. This naturally drives kinetic decoupling to earlier times, even away from resonance. Starting from the full inelastic collision operator, we derive an effective momentum transfer rate for kinetic decoupling. We then solve the coupled Boltzmann equations for the dark matter abundance, its temperature $T_χ$, and the $B-L$ asymmetry. Early kinetic decoupling can significantly modify the relic abundance, although near resonance this modification can be reduced by annihilation-induced heating. The $B-L$ asymmetry can be affected when asymmetry production overlaps with a substantial departure from kinetic equilibrium. In our scan, the largest deviations occur mainly for $x_{\rm lep}\gtrsim x_{\rm cd}$. After imposing our constraints, asymmetry production typically ends before chemical decoupling, leaving the final asymmetry essentially unchanged. For indirect detection, we generate the photon spectrum with Pythia and evaluate the Fermi-LAT dwarf spheroidal likelihood.

title: Gravitational Dark Matter Production from Spectator Field in $R^2$-Higgs Inflation
comment: 20 pages, 7 figures, 2 tables
summary: We investigate the cosmological gravitational dark matter production of spectator field $χ$ in the multifield $R^2$-Higgs inflation. The spectator field $χ$ couples to gravity only through a non-minimal coupling $ξ_χχ^2R$ and serves as a dark matter (DM) candidate. Working consistently in the Einstein frame, we derive the equation of motion of the background fields and fluctuations at linear order using the doubly covariant formalism. We show the dark matter production and the subsequent comoving relic abundance heavily depend on this effective mass of the field $χ$. Specifically, we find that there exists cancellation regions in the effective mass-squared of $χ$, which ensures the correct relic abundance is achieved. Further, we show that the preheating from Higgs and Goldstone may play critical role in accounting the observed relic density.

title: Machine Learning Based Classification of Type 1 Active Galactic Nuclei
comment: 14 Figures, 3 tables, accepted for publication in A&A
summary: Aims. We aim to provide a machine learning based method to distinguish type 1 quasars and type 1 Seyfert galaxies based on photometric data, which could be applied to large all-sky surveys. The method can also be used to obtain relatively complete samples of Seyfert galaxy candidates when broad-line AGNs have been selected. Results. The results of PCA show that quasars and Seyfert galaxies are partial distinguishable. The supervised classifier based on random forest (RF) achieves good performances for type 1 quasars with a F1 score of 0.967. The performance for classifying Seyfert galaxies is worse, with a F1 score of 0.791. Increasing the classification threshold can help to derive a sample of Seyfert galaxies with high purity. The classifier are then applied to the cross-matched sample with DESI DR1. When compared with the results of spectroscopic classification, quasars also show high precision and recall. For Seyfert galaxies identified by RF classifier, there are plenty of less luminous sources who are classified as quasars by spectroscopic method. If they are regarded as Seyfert galaxies, our classifier also performs well to predict Seyfert galaxies. Both the median SEDs and the fraction of Seyfert galaxies derived by our classifier are similar with those for the training sample, while the fraction of Seyfert galaxies for spectroscopic classification are lower at all redshift. These results indicate that our classifier can recover the features of Seyfert galaxies, at least those similar to the Seyfert galaxies in the training sample.

title: Unveiling the Shock-Excited Molecular Environment in the Orion Protostar HOPS 370
comment: 4 figures, 12 pages; accepted for publication in the Journal of Astrophysics and Astronomy (JoAA)
summary: We present near-infrared K-band ($1.94$--$2.52~μ$m) spectroscopy of the deeply embedded protostellar source HOPS\,370, obtained with the TIFR--ARIES Near Infrared Spectrometer (TANSPEC) on the 3.6-m Devasthal Optical Telescope (DOT). The spectrum is dominated by prominent molecular hydrogen ($\rm H_2$) ro-vibrational emission, with multiple transitions detected from the $1$--$0$ S, $2$--$1$ S, and $1$--$0$ Q branches. Using the intrinsically linked $\rm H_2$ $1$--$0$ Q(3) and $1$--$0$ S(1) transitions, which arise from the same upper energy level, we derive a visual extinction of $A_V = 23.24 \pm 1.25$ mag, corresponding to $A_K = 2.50 \pm 0.13$ mag, consistent with the embedded Class~0/I nature of the source. The diagnostic line ratio $F(2$--$1~{\rm S}(1))/F(1$--$0~{\rm S}(1)) = 0.12 \pm 0.01$ is consistent with thermal excitation and disfavors ultraviolet fluorescence as the dominant excitation mechanism. Assuming optically thin emission and local thermodynamic equilibrium, we derive an $\rm H_2$ excitation diagram that yields an excitation temperature of $2078 \pm 215$ K and a molecular hydrogen column density of $(1.93 \pm 0.93)\times10^{20}$ cm$^{-2}$. We further derive an ortho-to-para ratio of $2.45 \pm 0.21$, indicating substantial shock-driven thermal processing while remaining below the high-temperature equilibrium value of 3. Taken together, these diagnostics indicate that the molecular hydrogen emission in HOPS\,370 originates predominantly in warm, shock-heated gas most likely associated with its protostellar outflow. Our results demonstrate the diagnostic power of combined S- and Q-branch $\rm H_2$ spectroscopy for constraining the physical conditions and excitation history of deeply embedded protostellar systems.

title: Model of the instrumental polarization induced by a rotating HWP with anti-reflective sub-wavelength structures for CMB polarimetry
summary: Future CMB polarization experiments require precise control of instrumental systematics in the search for primordial $B$-mode polarization. A rotating half-wave plate (HWP) provides effective polarization modulation, but its non-ideal electromagnetic response can generate HWP-synchronous instrumental polarization. In this work, we characterize the response of a multi-layer sapphire HWP with anti-reflective sub-wavelength structures (SWS) using rigorous coupled-wave analysis. For three asymmetric SWS models, we find no substantial differences in the transmittance, polarization efficiency, or instrumental-polarization response that can be attributed to the type of SWS asymmetry. The fourth-harmonic instrumental polarization relevant to CMB polarization reconstruction is typically of order $10^{-4}$ in the CMB bands, which is expected to be mitigated. We further evaluate an actually fabricated SWS geometry, whose asymmetry enhances the retardance, and compare its response with that of an idealized model having the same type of asymmetry. Comparison of the realistic SWS with the idealized model shows that higher transmittance tends to be associated with lower instrumental polarization. These results suggest that improving the total transmission, including the effect of the fabricated SWS profile, may be more important for reducing HWP-induced instrumental polarization than tuning the SWS asymmetry itself.

title: Core-collapse universality for inelastic self-interacting dark matter halos
comment: 35 total pages, 7 figures. 24 pages of main text and 11 pages of appendices
summary: We study the gravothermal collapse of inelastic dark matter halos with velocity-dependent elastic and dissipative self-interactions. Within the gravothermal fluid framework, we derive the effective cooling rate for dark matter upscattering to an excited state followed by decay back to the ground state, with emitted states carrying off energy from the halo. We solve the gravothermal fluid equations numerically to simulate spherically symmetric halos over the core-growing and collapse phases of their evolution. While halos with purely elastic self-interactions have universal evolution trajectories, inelastic dark matter halos exhibit much more diversity in their evolution. Nevertheless, inelastic halo dynamics contain a hidden parametric universality from which we derive a semi-analytic formula for calculating the halo collapse time for arbitrary velocity-dependent elastic and inelastic cross sections without the need for simulations.

title: Kinematic methods of spiral nature identification: limitations and applicability
comment: 17 pages, 11 figures, accepted in MNRAS
summary: The nature of spiral arms in galaxies remains debated, with several competing formation scenarios, including density waves, kinematic spirals, dynamic spirals, and recurrent modes, that are difficult to distinguish observationally. We tested two kinematic methods - the phase reversal method and the velocity harmonic dominance method - using toy models and mock data from TNG50 simulations. For bar resonances, the phase reversal method is strongly orientation-dependent and yields reliable corotation estimates only when the bar is aligned with the disc minor axis. For spiral arms, the phase reversal method does not always yield reliable results and should be used in tondem with another kinematic method. The velocity harmonic dominance method is more robust: it distinguishes between density wave, kinematic, and dynamic spiral patterns, although it still shows some sensitivity to orientation. Uncertainties in the rotation curve do not strongly affect its results. We also apply both methods to the observed grand-design spiral galaxy NGC3938 as an illustrative example; the results suggest the presence of multiple spiral modes, consistent with the recurrent modes scenario and this interpretation relies on different indirect evidence. Based on our findings, we propose a strategy for classifying spiral structure in observed galaxies that combines multiple independent tests. Applying this analysis to an extended sample will allow us to validate its predictive power and to investigate the diversity of spiral formation scenarios.

title: GRAVITY-RESOLVE: A comprehensive image reconstruction tool for Galactic Center observations with GRAVITY
comment: Submitted to Astronomy & Astrophysics (A&A) on October 24, 2026
summary: We aim to improve and extend the imaging capabilities of the GRAVITY beam combiner instrument of ESOs VLTI with respect to reconstruction software in the Galactic Center. We revise and develop the image reconstruction code GRAVITY-RESOLVE $\text{G}^{\text{R}}$, which has been specifically developed to reconstruct stars in the Galactic Center with GRAVITY. The main objectives are to increase the limiting magnitude in GRAVITY images, reduce its computational runtime, and allow for a joint reconstruction of multiple, spatially separate datasets/pointings on sky. We apply $\text{G}^{\text{R}}$ to recent GRAVITY data, featuring the implemented GRAVITY-faint mode as part of GRAVITY+, the upgrade of GRAVITY. We reconstruct visibility phases and amplitudes and present the first GRAVITY image reconstructed with $\text{G}^{\text{R}}$ from these quantities. We demonstrate NIR mosaicking with $\text{G}^{\text{R}}$ by jointly reconstructing nine separately acquired datasets of 2025 into a single image on a scale of $\simeq 3390\ \text{AU}\times 3390\ \text{AU}$, corresponding to $409.6\ \text{mas}\times 409.6\ \text{mas}$. With dedicated injection tests of point sources into GRAVITY data, we estimate the limiting magnitude to be $m_{\text{K}}\ \simeq\ 20.0$ within a radius of $25\ \text{mas}$ around the field center when reconstructing from closure phases and visibility amplitudes. We report on the discovery of two new faint stars in the Galactic Center: S303 and S304. Finally, we find a decrease in computational runtime by a factor of at least $\sim10$. With $\text{G}^{\text{R}}$, we demonstrate GRAVITYs capabilities for NIR imaging. We show that $\text{G}^{\text{R}}$ is a fast, precise, and deep image reconstruction tool for Galactic Center observations, enabling the discovery of even more faint stars.

title: Understanding the origin of silver in metal-poor stars based on the non-local thermodynamic equilibrium analysis of Ag I lines
comment: 12 pages, four tables, seven figures; accepted for publication in the Astrophysical Journal
summary: Silver is a poorly observed neutron-capture element, and understanding its Galactic production history requires accurate abundances for stellar samples covering a broad metallicity range. We refined the method for calculating stellar Ag abundances by considering the non-local thermodynamic equilibrium (NLTE) line formation for Ag I. A comprehensive model atom of silver was built from the atomic data available in the literature, including recent data on inelastic Ag I + H I collisions. We derived abundances using the high-resolution spectra and the synthetic spectrum method with the one-dimensional model atmospheres. From two Ag I lines in the solar spectrum we obtained the NLTE abundances log epsilon = 1.15 and 1.10 for different treatments of collisions with hydrogen atoms. The NLTE abundances of Ag were determined for the first time for 41 stars in the -2.74 <= [Fe/H] <= -0.56 metallicity range. The NLTE abundance corrections for Ag I 3382 A were found to be larger for the giants (up to 0.92~dex) than the dwarfs (up to 0.51~dex). In NLTE, Ag in our sample stars is enhanced relatively to Fe and the [Ag/Fe] Galactic trend is very similar to that for [Eu/Fe]; the [Ag/Eu], [Ag/Ba], and [Ag/Sr] abundance ratios of the r-II stars CS22892-052 and CS31082-001 agree very well with the r-process model of Prantzos et al. (2020); the -1.6 < [Fe/H] <= -0.56 stars have close-to-solar [Ag/Eu] ratios. We conclude that production of silver was dominated by the main r-process throughout the metallicity range we investigated, with the main s-process contribution of not larger than 20% for [Fe/H] > -1.6.

title: Nongravitational Motion of 3I/ATLAS Far from the Sun: Robust Detection, Weak Constraints on the Activity Law
comment: 11 pages, 2 figures, accepted for publication in Astronomy & Astrophysics
summary: 3I/ATLAS provides an unprecedented astrometric data set for studying nongravitational (NG) effects in an interstellar object, but existing orbital solutions depend strongly on assumptions regarding the heliocentric activity law and the treatment of the astrometric data. We investigate the extent to which astrometric observations constrain the heliocentric dependence of the NG activity function, focusing on the identifiability of different functional forms of $g(r)$ within standard NG orbit-determination frameworks. Astrometric observations obtained at heliocentric distances larger than 3.49 au before perihelion and 2.67 au after perihelion were analysed. Purely gravitational and nongravitational orbital solutions were determined using several activity laws, including the standard water-ice sublimation law and flatter more volatile ice prescriptions. The resulting residual distributions were evaluated using normality tests and analyses of temporal trends in the observed-minus-calculated residuals. The distant pre-perihelion observations are well described by a purely gravitational (GR) orbit, whereas the distant post-perihelion data exhibit a statistically significant non-Gaussian residual distribution under the GR model. When the distant pre- and post-perihelion observations are combined, nongravitational acceleration becomes clearly detectable through a significant reduction in the residual rms and the disappearance of systematic residual trends. However, the astrometric data do not uniquely distinguish between the tested activity laws: standard water-ice, more volatile and extreme volatile prescriptions produce statistically comparable orbital fits despite their markedly different heliocentric dependences. The existence of nongravitational acceleration is therefore considerably better constrained by astrometry than its physical origin or heliocentric dependence.

title: PyMsOfa 2.0: A Pure-Python Implementation of the IAU Standards of Fundamental Astronomy Service
comment: 9 pages, 3 figures
summary: Astrometric calculations require authoritative algorithms so that every result is correct and reproducible. The Standards of Fundamental Astronomy (SOFA) service of the International Astronomical Union (IAU) provides such algorithms, officially released only in Fortran 77 and ANSI C. In an earlier paper we presented the first version of PyMsOfa, a Python package wrapping the SOFA C library. Here we present PyMsOfa 2.0, which re-implements the complete SOFA library in pure Python with NumPy. All 247 official SOFA routines are ported directly to Python, requiring no compilation of any external C library and running identically on Linux, Windows, and macOS. The routines operate on NumPy arrays, so arguments can be processed in batch, which is convenient for survey pipelines and Monte Carlo simulations. The package also provides an extension module with validated models not yet part of the official SOFA release, such as the improved precession--nutation model IAU 2006$_{J_2}$/2000A$_{R26}$. The reimplementation reproduces the official SOFA algorithms: all constants, series, and coefficients are taken unchanged from the SOFA source files, and routine names differ only by the pym prefix. We verify every routine against the official SOFA C release: most reproduce the C results to machine precision, the remainder within the accuracy tolerance stated in the SOFA documentation. The package has been applied to Gaia astrometric reduction and used in astrometric studies of the Closeby Habitable Exoplanet Survey (CHES) mission, and is available through PyPI, GitHub, and Zenodo.

title: Numerical Simulations of the interaction between winds from tidal disruption event and supermassive black hole circumnuclear medium
comment: 25 pages, 15 figures, accepted by APJ
summary: The interaction between winds from tidal disruption event (TDE) and the circumnuclear medium (CNM) around supermassive black holes is believed to contribute to the radio emission of non-jetted TDEs. This model has been studied both analytically and numerically. In previous works, the properties of wind are usually set to be angle-independent. It is not clear to what extent the results deviate from those in the case where TDE wind properties are angle-dependent. We perform numerical simulations to investigate the effects of the angular distribution of wind properties on the radio light curve in the wind-CNM interaction model. We find that given that the wind mass and kinetic energy fixed, the radio light curve in the optically thin waveband significantly depends on the angle-dependence of wind properties. Even when the swept-up CNM mass is still less than the wind mass, a slight deceleration can affect the light curve. Changing the angular dependence of the wind properties causes the deceleration to vary across angles. Consequently, the final light curve--the time evolution of radiation integrated over all angles--would differ significantly from that predicted in models with a spatially uniform wind injection. This can result in a slower rise or a faster decline (depending on the CNM profile) than the analytical prediction, and can even turn the rise phase into a long-lasting plateau. Therefore, it is essential to carefully take into account the angular dependence of wind properties to study the wind-CNM interaction.

title: Turbulent gas-rich discs at high redshift: Chaotic orbits and rapid bulge formation at high gas fraction
comment: 14 pages, 9 figures. Submitted to MNRAS
summary: Using the \nexus\ N-body/hydrodynamic framework, we show that stellar bars that emerge in high-redshift disc galaxies are different in their orbital characteristics compared to their low-redshift counterparts. We identify bar-supporting orbits and, among them, find the fraction of chaotic orbits compared to regular orbits ($f_{\rm chaos}$). This fraction rises above 60\% for models with $f_{\rm gas} > 60 \%$; for $f_{\rm gas} \lesssim 60\%$, we observe chaotic fractions close to zero. The emerging bars seen in the $f_{\rm gas}= 80\%$ and $100\%$ simulations collapse in $\lesssim$1 Gyr to form central bulges supported by rotation, and this collapse follows soon after the chaotic fraction starts to dominate ($f_{\rm chaos} \gtrsim 50\%)$. Moreover, the gravitational potential in those simulations steepens rapidly over that period, and by integrating the chaotic orbits, we find that orbits that deviate from the evolving mean field are more likely to be chaotic. Hence, we argue that the irregularity associated with the rapidly evolving, central potentials drives higher chaotic fractions in these gas-rich bars. As a result, the emergent bars collapse through `violent relaxation' to form oblate rotating bulges. Supporting evidence for this picture comes from the fact that particles of different mass share identical radial profiles, a natural consequence of the rapid relaxation process.

title: Tidal shells as clocks of galaxy mergers and tests of cosmological models
comment: 10 pages, 7 figures; Proceedings IAU Symposium No. 403, The Hidden Beauty of the Galactic Outskirts
summary: Stellar shells-concentric arc-like tidal features formed in galaxy mergers-provide a valuable record of recent galaxy assembly histories encoding both the merger event and the gravitational potential of the host galaxy. We compare shell systems in observations and cosmological simulations from two complementary perspectives. First, we show that simulations predict a substantial population of very large (>100kpc) shells that are rarely observed, revealing a potentially important discrepancy between simulations and reality. Because the scales of observed and simulated shell systems differ significantly, we focus on a comparison of merger histories. Using a shell-identification method, we estimate merger times for a sample of nearby massive prolate rotators and compare them with merger histories derived from cosmological simulations. We also present ongoing efforts to expand the sample of deeply imaged prolate rotators using observations from the Milankovic telescope, paving the way for future studies based on larger observational samples.

title: Simulating and Characterizing Non-Gaussian Small-Scale Polarized Emission
comment: 25 pages, 19 figures, submitted to APJ
summary: Galactic foregrounds present a major challenge for cosmic microwave background (CMB) cosmology as their amplitudes exceed the target primordial $B$-mode signal. While small-scale interstellar medium (ISM) emission is expected to be highly complex, current foreground simulations cannot reproduce the filamentary, non-Gaussian features of ISM structure in a stochastic way. To address this gap, we introduce a framework for generating stochastic small-scale foreground emission, using polarized synchrotron observations as an example use case. This method is capable of producing many independent realizations that additionally inherit morphological information from large angular scales. The underlying structural complexity incorporates anisotropic, multifractal, and advected non-Gaussian features that are tunable with a small number of parameters that carry physical interpretations. Because standard power spectra do not describe the complex phase coherence required for the structural complexity, we evaluate the synthetic fields using higher-order statistics, demonstrating that the Minkowski functionals and structure functions partially capture varying degrees of non-Gaussianity. This work lays the necessary foundation for new foreground simulation suites with stochastic realizations of possible non-Gaussian structure.

title: Validating an X-ray-based method for identifying Fermi blazars
summary: Context. Blazars are the main population of active galactic nuclei (AGNs) detected in gamma rays by Fermi. However, around 34% of Fermi sources remain unidentified, partly due to their large positional uncertainties, motivating multiwavelength methods to identify possible counterparts. Aims. We evaluate a method proposed to identify BL Lacertae (BL Lac) candidates among unidentified Fermi sources based on their X-ray properties, using Swift-XRT observations. Methods. We examined published optical spectra for an initial sample of 148 X-ray-selected candidates. We found 71 sources with spectra spatially consistent with the proposed associations and reassessed their classifications using standard blazar criteria. We then compared these classifications with the method's initial predictions. Results. Of the 71 proposed counterparts, 80.28% are classified as BL Lac objects and 87.32% as possible gamma-ray-emitting AGNs, supporting the effectiveness of the X-ray-based selection. We also identify four Seyfert galaxies, suggesting that the method is sensitive to this class despite its rarity among gamma-ray emitters. Conclusions. Our results show that X-ray observations are effective for selecting BL Lac candidates among unidentified Fermi sources and support future spectroscopic follow-up campaigns. The high fraction of BL Lacs and AGNs suggests that blazars may account for a substantial part of the unidentified gamma-ray population. The Seyfert identifications also raise questions about the origin of high-energy emission in AGNs not typically associated with relativistic jets, highlighting the need for further multiwavelength observations.

title: No Significant Excess in Typical Variability in CLAS+ Changing-Look AGN Candidates in Rubin DP2
summary: Rubin Data Preview 2 (DP2) samples the CLAS+ changing-look AGN (CLAGN) candidates $\sim1,000-9,000$ days after their comparison epochs, so it can test whether these objects retain enhanced short-term optical variability after their spectral transitions. Comparing peak-to-peak amplitude in magnitudes against a photometrically quiescent quasar control, one band at a time, we do not detect a significant median-amplitude excess for any state (turn-on, turn-off, intermediate) in either of two bands, nor a different in the median $\,|\,Δ\text{mag}\,|\,$ as function of time lag. The $r$-band CLAS+ amplitude distributions are wider than the control's, with the intermediate state formally significant after multiple-comparison correction. This could hint for a high-amplitude subpopulation.

title: Combining Multiple Incomplete Astronomical Surveys to Estimate Galaxy Flux Distributions
comment: 35 pages, 10 figures, 6 tables; includes supplementary material
summary: In astrophysics, the distributions of fluxes or intensities of populations of sources provide insight into the structure and evolution of the universe. We propose a science-driven hierarchical Bayesian framework to estimate the X-ray flux distribution of a population of galaxies. The distribution is parameterized via a broken power law model, formulated as a mixture of Pareto distributions, and is fit using data from a combination of non-representative X-ray and optical surveys. Because fainter sources are less likely to be detected, astronomical surveys suffer from incompleteness at the low-intensity end, and dedicated survey simulations are used to study the resulting missing-data pattern and determine the form of corrections. We introduce a methodology to combine data from two (or more) surveys with different incompleteness functions. This allows us to leverage deeper surveys (e.g., optical) to more fully characterize the X-ray log(N)-log(S) (where fewer sources are detected). We take advantage of a well-calibrated characterization of the missing-data pattern, particularly in X-ray surveys, to make incompleteness corrections for sources that are not detected in either survey. The proposed model is validated using a simulation study designed to mimic the Chandra Deep Field South (CDF-S), demonstrating accurate recovery of the flux distribution even under high proportions of systematic incompleteness. Finally, we apply our proposed method to data from the CDF-S.

title: Primordial Gravitational Waves in Loop Quantum Cosmology: Regularization Ambiguities and Initial State Dependence
comment: 34 pages, 11 figures
summary: We compute the primordial tensor power spectrum in standard loop quantum cosmology and in the modified models mLQC-I and mLQC-II, evolving the tensor perturbations across the bounce in the hybrid and dressed metric prescriptions with a Starobinsky potential. In mLQC-I, the emergent de Sitter contracting branch requires the use of dedicated initial states. We use de Sitter mode function in the dressed metric approach and a Hankel-function solution in the hybrid approach. For inflationary e-foldings $N_e = 60$ and $65$, the pivot-scale tensor-to-scalar ratio agrees with the value of standard inflation with this potential. The scale-dependent ratio $r(k)=\mathcal{P}_T/\mathcal{P}_S$ cancels effects common to the two sectors and separates features that are independent of the initial state from those that depend on it. It varies slowly in the scale-invariant regime and oscillates around $r_\star$ at smaller $k$. The oscillations next to the scale-invariant regime do not depend on the adiabatic order, unlike the peaks and spikes at lower $k$. For a given initial state, the regularization dependence survives in the infrared, where long-wavelength modes retain a record of the bounce and of the pre-bounce branch. We propagate the normalized spectra to the CMB $B$-mode spectrum and discuss observational prospects.

title: Disentangling constraints on $S_8$ from the high and low redshift CMB
comment: 9 pages, 5 figures
summary: The clustering of matter in the universe is quantified by $σ_8$, the RMS fluctuations today in linear theory in spheres of radius $8h^{-1}$ Mpc, where $h$ parametrizes the Hubble constant. Surveys of gravitational lensing and galaxy clustering best constrain $S_8\equiv (Ω_m/0.3)^{0.5} σ_8$, where $Ω_m$ is the energy density of matter in units of the critical density. Comparing this late time measurement to the value of $S_8$ inferred from the cosmic microwave background (CMB), one can test the $Λ$CDM prediction for the growth of clustering from the primordial universe to now. Several analyses report hints that CMB measurements of $S_8$ are larger than those from galaxy surveys. However, CMB measurements have information from both high and low redshift due to lensing, and these tests traditionally conflate the two. Here, we present a technique to extract constraints on the cosmological parameters from each redshift component separately, enabling a high-z vs. low-z clustering comparison that was not previously possible. We marginalize over lensing information using a principal component analysis, and show that the primordial CMB from combined Planck 2018, ACT DR6, and SPT-3G D1 prefers $S_8= 0.795\pm0.022$, in agreement with the recent determination from the Dark Energy Survey (DES) of $S_8=0.789\pm0.012$. The clustering inferred from CMB lensing is larger. However, both the level of excess lensing and increase in agreement with DES depends on the prior on the sum of neutrino masses, $\sum m_ν$. We find that removing lensing brings the CMB towards agreement with DES in any case.

title: The Redshift-Space Cluster-Galaxy Cross-Correlation as a Probe of Gravity on Cosmic Scales
summary: Testing General Relativity (GR) on cosmological scales requires probes that are directly sensitive to gravitational dynamics. We present a Fisher matrix forecast of how well the Dark Energy Spectroscopic Instrument (DESI) Bright Galaxy Survey (BGS) can constrain departures from GR through the cluster infall velocity field, using the redshift-space cluster-galaxy cross-correlation function $ξ^{\rm s}_{\rm cg}(r_p, r_π)$ as the primary observable. We construct mock catalogs from the AbacusSummit N-body simulations, using a Halo Occupation Distribution (HOD) model for galaxies and a log-normal mass-observable relation for cluster selection. We parameterize departures from GR with a single multiplicative factor $F_{\rm G}$ that rescales halo infall velocities relative to the GR prediction. Marginalizing over the HOD, mass-observable, and cosmological parameters, we find that DESI BGS can constrain $F_{\rm G}$ to $σ(F_{\rm G}) = 0.033$ at $z \sim 0.3$. This precision is sufficient to distinguish representative $f(R)$ and Galileon gravity models from GR at $\gtrsim 4σ$. The strongest limitation is a degeneracy between $F_{\rm G}$ and the scatter in the cluster mass-observable relation, while the constraint shows no strong degeneracy with any individual HOD parameter. Perfect knowledge of the galaxy-halo connection would improve the constraint to $σ(F_{\rm G}) \approx 0.015$, and including the galaxy autocorrelation function in the data vector could recover part of this improvement. The same data vector yields tight constraints on the cosmological parameters, $σ(Ω_m) = 0.010$ and $σ(σ_8) = 0.010$, only moderately correlated with $F_{\rm G}$. These results demonstrate the potential of DESI BGS cluster-galaxy correlations to test gravity on quasi-linear scales, complementary to existing modified gravity probes and to weak-lensing cluster mass profiles.

title: The nature of the Norma arm as a bar-driven star-forming shock front
summary: The Milky Way is commonly depicted as having four major spiral arms, including the Norma-Outer arm, and a central stellar bar whose properties remain debated. Masers associated with young high-mass stars have been used to trace a segment of the "Norma arm" extending from one end of the Galaxy's central stellar bar. Recent work suggests that these masers may reside along a spiral arm or occupy the dominant x1 stellar orbits that give the bar its shape. We now use a new generation of N-body, hydrodynamic simulations to argue that these million-year old masers instead trace the Galactic bar's Quadrant I shock front or, equivalently, its dust lane. This implies that the bar dust-lane is star-forming, shedding new light on our understanding of star formation processes in the Milky Way. By associating the masers with the simulated shock front, we determine the bar's parameters to be: a ~ 4.3 +/- 0.2 kpc, b ~ 2.3 +/- 0.2 kpc, phi = 20 (+5/-2) deg, Omega_p <~ 40 km s^-1 kpc^-1, representing the bar's semi-major and semi-minor half-lengths, inclination angle and pattern speed, respectively. This raises questions about the Milky Way's spiral structure and suggests that the Galactic bar is long, slow and star-forming.

title: Migration Traps as Variability Attractors. II. Nonmonotonic X-Ray Timing Signatures of Embedded Stellar-Mass Black Holes in AGN Disks
comment: 12 pages, 3 figures, 2 tables
summary: Stellar-mass black holes (sBHs) embedded in active galactic nucleus (AGN) disks may affect X-ray variability through magnetic reconnection. As sBHs migrate and accumulate near migration traps, they disturb the disk magnetic field and trigger reconnection events that heat the disk and eject plasma into the overlying corona. The injected plasma dissipates kinetic energy and can trigger the release of magnetic energy already stored in the corona. We calculate the resulting coronal X-ray emission and the disk ultraviolet (UV) variability, including the disk thermal response and reprocessing of incident X-rays. We find that embedded sBHs can initially enhance short-timescale X-ray variability, but the variability becomes suppressed as more sBHs accumulate in the disk. At higher mass accretion rates through AGN disks, this suppression appears earlier. As sBH-associated reconnection events become more frequent, their active regions increasingly overlap, reducing the magnetic energy available to each event from the corona. We also find that variations in the disk ultraviolet (UV) emission follow the X-ray variations with a shorter delay than in the model without sBHs. These results suggest that a growing population of embedded sBHs does not necessarily produce stronger short-timescale X-ray variability.

title: Early Dark Energy Crowds Out Interacting Dark Energy
comment: 35 pages, 5 figures, 4 tables
summary: We investigate whether interacting dark energy can provide additional relief to the Hubble tension once early dark energy (EDE) is present. Considering a cosmology containing EDE, an independent late-time dark energy fluid with an equation of state fixed at $w\simeq-1$ interacting with cold dark matter, and a cosmological constant, we find that the data strongly drive the model toward the non-interacting limit. The best fit effectively reduces to the standard EDE cosmology, where a non-zero EDE component provides most of the required increase in $H_0$, leaving little statistical gain for the interaction. Although energy transfer from dark matter to dark energy can raise $H_0$ further, this limited gain is rapidly outweighed by the deterioration of the fit to low-redshift observations. In particular, since the CMB tightly constrains the early-time physical matter density, any additional energy transfer requires a lower present-day matter abundance. Such low values are strongly disfavored by Type Ia supernovae. We show that this limitation becomes particularly severe once EDE has already raised $H_0$ and that the same mechanism extends to a broad class of post-recombination interactions. Allowing a dynamical dark energy equation of state of the Chevallier-Polarski-Linder form does not alter our conclusions.

title: Simulation-Informed Dust Masses in Typical $6<z<14$ JWST Galaxies
comment: 8 pages, 5 figures, submitted to ApJL, comments welcome
summary: Direct detections of dust in typical $z>8$ galaxies remain untenable, despite the presence of dust suggested by rest-frame UV/optical spectro-photometry. Informed by cosmological zoom-in simulations where dust particles evolve on-the-fly, we present a novel method for inferring dust masses in high-redshift galaxies using stellar half-light radii and UV/optical attenuation. Our methods reproduce observed trends at lower redshift, ultimately diverging from Milky Way-based calibration factors by up to $\sim1.5$ dex. We apply this method to observed JWST galaxies from $6<z<14$, and find dust masses in the range $M_{\rm dust}\sim10^3-10^5\,M_\odot$ that are fully consistent with upper limits from ALMA, and suggest an early dust enrichment period by supernovae followed by efficient grain destruction in the hot gas. Future observations may use our tabulated calibration to infer dust masses over a wide range of stellar masses and redshifts.

title: Atmospheric Parameter Determination of RR Lyrae Stars With Mephisto Multi-band Photometry
summary: Phase-resolved atmospheric parameters of pulsating stars, including RR Lyrae stars and Cepheids, are essential for studying stellar structure and pulsation physics and for establishing accurate stellar benchmarks for Galactic structure and assembly history. We present a photometric framework that simultaneously infers Teff, log g, and [Fe/H] from Mephisto multi-epoch, multi-band (u, v, g, r, i, z) photometry. A supervised neural-network forward model is built by training on synthetic colors derived from theoretical stellar atmosphere models. It reproduces the synthetic colors to a precision of 0.01 per cent. The model is applied to observed multi-epoch colors to derive phase-dependent atmospheric parameters. We apply the method to six RRab and four RRc stars in three globular clusters observed with Mephisto. We find typical per-phase uncertainties of about 62 K in effective temperature (Teff), 0.10 dex in surface gravity (log g), and 0.16 dex in metallicity ([Fe/H]). Repeated measurements across the pulsation cycle reduce the typical formal uncertainty of the final [Fe/H] estimates to roughly 0.03 dex. A sensitivity analysis indicates that the five Mephisto colors provide distinct and complementary constraints on the three stellar atmospheric parameters: (u-v) provides robust constraints on log g, (v-g) is informative for estimating [Fe/H], and (u-v), (v-g), (g-r), (r-i), and (i-z) all provide information on Teff. The results demonstrate that Mephisto multi-epoch, multi-band photometry can deliver precise, cost-effective phase-resolved atmospheric parameters for RR Lyrae stars, offering an efficient way to construct large samples of stellar benchmarks for studies of stellar pulsation physics and Galactic structure and evolution.

title: The Influence of Hubble Expansion on the Future Merger of the Milky Way and Andromeda
comment: 10 pages (+3 pages appendix). Accepted for publication in ApJ
summary: Most existing idealized simulations of galaxy mergers neglect Hubble expansion, as the local Hubble flow is curved by overdensities and the expansion effect is weak at these scales. However, even in the gravity-dominated Local Group (LG), the expansion itself still persists, and it has been shown important in some LG-related studies. Here we take the future merger of the Milky Way (MW) and Andromeda (M31) as a case study to investigate the differences between simulations with and without Hubble expansion. We perform a suite of idealized N-body simulations of the MW--M31 system under pure Newtonian, $Λ$CDM, and $w_0w_a$CDM scenarios, testing different masses and proper motions of galaxies informed by current observational constraints. At low M31 tangential velocities, especially in cases where the two galaxies merge within a Hubble time, the expansion effect is negligible; while at high velocities (>66.5 km/s), the $Λ$CDM simulations introduce a noticeable delay in the merger time compared to the Newtonian ones and may even alter the final fate of the system, but the caveat here is that the isolated-pair idealization and the assumed expansion history break down. The delay is also present but less pronounced in the $w_0w_a$CDM runs. When M33 and the Large Magellanic Cloud are included, the differences in merger times are reduced. In summary, Hubble expansion can play a noticeable role for galaxy mergers with high tangential velocities, but its actual influence on the MW--M31 merger depends on the precise masses and proper motions to be determined in the future.

title: Age-Resolved Vertical Motions in the Milky Way Warp: A Localized Enhancement in Intermediate-Age Populations
comment: 13 pages, 6 figures, 1 table, accepted for publication in ApJL. Online Dataset: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23308202
summary: Determining how the Milky Way warp evolves provides constraints on the formation and dynamical evolution of galactic disks. Using Apache Point Observatory Galactic Evolution Experiment Data Release 19 (APOGEE DR19) spectroscopy, we estimate ages for 222,355 red giants. With Gaia astrometry and geometric distances, we analyze 168,824 of these stars in five age bins spanning $0$--$10$ Gyr. The warp-related radial vertical-velocity ($V_Z$) profile of young red giants ($0$--$2$ Gyr) is broadly consistent with those of classical Cepheids and young open clusters. Over $9\leq R<12$ kpc, we find that the mean $V_Z$ values of the intermediate-age red giants ($2$--$4$ and $4$--$6$ Gyr) are $1.48\pm0.46$ and $1.49\pm0.52$ km s$^{-1}$ higher than that of the young population, respectively. By contrast, at $R\simeq12$--$13$ kpc, the $V_Z$ profiles of the $0$--$6$ Gyr red giants are consistent within their uncertainties. The intermediate-age enhancement persists across our robustness tests and may reflect smaller effective kinematic warp onset radii for the intermediate-age populations. The observed velocity differences may arise from the combined effects of earlier perturbations and the present-day warp, or from differences in vertical structure among stellar populations.

title: Gravitational Wave Background from Metastable Current-Carrying Cosmic Strings
comment: 44 pages, 14 figures
summary: We study the stochastic gravitational wave background (SGWB) generated by networks of current-carrying metastable cosmic strings (MSCSs). Extending previous studies, we include the possibility of vorton formation phenomenologically. We construct an analytical template that provides a fast and accurate approximation to the spectrum in the frequency range probed by pulsar timing arrays (PTAs). We also show how the parameters of cosmic string networks determine the low-frequency slope. For the frequency range relevant for LIGO-Virgo-KAGRA (LVK), we derive an analytical expression that constrains the scale-invariant part of the SGWB. Finally, we confront the model with current constraints from PTAs and the LVK collaboration. We identify regions of the parameter space that can produce a signal consistent with PTA observations but are in tension with LVK constraints, suggesting that additional mechanisms to suppress the high-frequency spectrum are required for a consistent interpretation of the PTA signal

title: The scale of homogeneity in DESI Data Release 1
comment: 19 pages, 11 figures, 5 tables. Submitted to the Publications of the Astronomical Society of Australia
summary: We present measurements of the scale of cosmic homogeneity using the first data release (DR1) of the Dark Energy Spectroscopic Instrument (DESI), the largest publicly available spectroscopic extragalactic survey to date. Using a counts-in-spheres estimator applied to nearly 5 million galaxies and quasars across six independent redshift bins spanning $0.1 < z < 2.1$, we measure the correlation dimension $D_2(r)$ and define the homogeneity scale $R_H$ as the point at which the galaxy distribution reaches within 1\% of the homogeneous asymptotic value. We find that all tracers clearly transition to homogeneity, with the galaxy homogeneity scale ranging from $93.8^{+0.9}_{-0.7}$ to $142.6^{+1.4}_{-1.4}$ $h^{-1}$Mpc depending on the tracer redshift, galaxy bias, and modelling used to extract the scale. Using a cosmology-dependent model, we reconstruct the underlying matter homogeneity scale, finding it decreases monotonically with redshift in excellent agreement with $Λ$CDM predictions. We identify a systematic offset of up to $\sim 10\%$ between measurements in the North and South Galactic Caps, largely due to fiber assignment effects reproduced in our simulations. Accounting for this, and with a complementary demonstration using toy models that our methodology correctly identifies inhomogeneous universes in all but rather finely-tuned observer configurations, this hence provides strong evidence in favour of the cosmological principle across our full redshift range. Our matter homogeneity scale measurements are consistent with, and substantially more precise than, previous constraints from WiggleZ and SDSS, demonstrating the power of DESI data for precision tests of the cosmological principle.

title: Cosmic rays in galaxy halos I: the circumgalactic transport rate and a dynamically significant cosmic-ray reservoir
comment: 18 pages of main text with 10 figures; 2 appendices. Constructive community feedback welcomed in advance of submission
summary: Fermi-LAT observations imply that most of the cosmic rays (CRs) produced in normal star-forming galaxies escape from the discs where they are accelerated into the circumgalactic medium (CGM), but the subsequent evolution of those escaping CRs is unclear. Here we construct a simple semi-analytic model for their transport and loss, which we constrain by confronting the model with a series of observations: limits on CR energy densities in the outer Milky Way from Fermi-LAT, the isotropic gamma-ray background (IGRB), stacked CGM X-ray emission from eROSITA, and the requirement that the accumulated pressure of CRs in galaxy CGMs not be so large as to render them unstable. We show that these constraints can be jointly satisfied in only two scenarios: one where CRs diffuse quickly through the CGM and freely escape beyond it into the IGM, and another where the CR diffusion time out of halos is of order the Hubble time. In the latter scenario CRs accelerated by star formation naturally explain both the IGRB and the heat input required to maintain the temperature of the CGM against X-ray cooling, and their relatively slow transport means that roughly half of the CR energy injected into the CGM of an $L_\star$ halo over its star-formation history remains there at $z \simeq 0$. This makes CR pressure dynamically significant, and also means that a non-negligible part of the IGRB is produced by CRs in the Milky Way's own halo. We argue that this latter scenario is the more likely one, as it avoids the need to posit a second source for the IGRB that is coincidentally very close in both power and spectral shape to the contribution from star-forming discs.

title: Probing Cosmology with Diffusion Models: Memorization, Generalization, and Parameter Estimation
comment: 6 pages, 3 figures. Accepted to the Machine Learning and the Physical Sciences Workshop 2026
summary: Diffusion models are increasingly used as surrogates for expensive cosmological simulations, but simple metrics like reconstruction fidelity do not guarantee a surrogate can be trusted for scientific inference. To explore this, we train diffusion models on HI fields from the CAMELS IllustrisTNG simulations and test how three properties change with training-set size: memorization of individual training examples, agreement with one- and two-point statistics (the pixel-value distribution and the power spectrum), and estimation of cosmological parameters from the generated fields. At fixed model size, generative models trained with smaller, less diverse training data produced memorized samples. While this is a well known phenomenon, we show that this leads to miscalibrated parameter densities for cosmological inference tasks. At fixed size, there is a training set size with enough information content to enable a model to generalize, at which point posterior density estimation with neural surrogates can be well-calibrated. We demonstrate that a neural surrogate can therefore pass visual, one-point and power-spectrum convergence tests while still resulting in overconfident parameter estimation in a cosmological inference pipeline. Thus, tests of model generalization should be an additional check for inference pipelines adopting neural surrogates.

title: Ejected and Rejected: Strong Scatterings in Dense Star Clusters
comment: Submitted to ApJ, Comments welcome!
summary: Understanding the evolution of collisional stellar systems is key to predicting both the bulk evolution of dense star clusters and also the rates of tidal disruption events, extreme mass ratio inspirals (EMRIs), stellar ejections, and other loss cone phenomena. Although a majority of the evolution is dictated by weak, small-angle scatterings, rare close encounters resulting in strong scatterings can sometimes produce qualitatively different outcomes. To systematically determine the astrophysical importance of strong scatterings, we derive the exact differential rate distribution of velocity kicks in isotropic and spherically symmetric distribution functions representing globular and nuclear star clusters, while also deriving the distribution boundaries and approximate rate scalings. We then extend this formalism to derive approximate rates of energy and angular momentum kicks for objects in the nuclear star cluster, and then apply this framework to study (i) ejections and (ii) ``cancellation'' of extreme mass ratio inspirals. We find that ejection rates are complicated in some regimes due to the saturation of the strong kick distribution and the breakdown of the weak limit, likely enhancing the effect of loss cone shielding. We also determine that a sizable fraction of proto-EMRIs will likely be canceled by strong scatterings, highlighting the need for future work to determine to what degree strong scatterings impact the true EMRI rate.

title: Not so dead after all: young stars in the massive S0 NGC 3115
comment: Accepted for publication in A&A, 12 pages, 6 figures, 2 appendix
summary: Context: Massive early-type galaxies (ETGs) are traditionally considered "red-and-dead" based on optical observations. However, ultraviolet (UV) spectroscopy can uncover a hidden population of young stars with a sub-one-per cent mass fraction. Aims: We measure the young stellar mass fraction in NGC 3115, a massive isolated lenticular galaxy, to test the ubiquity and spatial distribution of this component beyond previously studied ellipticals. Methods: Using SOAR/Goodman spectra and line-strength fitting, we modelled the star-formation history with a single bulk stellar population plus a young component (constant star-formation over the last 1 Gyr). We used ultranest to derive posterior distributions for age, metallicity, [Mg/Fe], and the young stellar mass fraction. Results: By tracking spatial variations in U-band indices, we found the young stellar mass fraction peaks at $0.69^{+0.09}_{-0.15}\%$ in the centre, dropping to zero beyond 1 kpc. This young component correlates with kinematic structures, dominating in the pressure-supported region. We interpret this as residual central star formation fueled by internal processes, such as recycled stellar material. Alternative UV-bright models (e.g., extreme horizontal branch stars) yielded poorer fits and unphysically high mass fractions. Conclusions: Young stars in old, "red-and-dead" galaxies are more common than expected. Their presence across various ETGs with similar gradients indicates that residual star formation is a ubiquitous feature, offering key constraints on the baryon cycle in these galaxies.

title: Extra! Extra! X-ray Emission!: X-rays in Romulus25, Part II - Physical Drivers of X-ray Emission in the CGM
comment: 10 pages, 9 figures, submitted to The Astrophysical Journal
summary: Characterizing the hot (T ~ 10$^{6}$ K) circumgalactic medium (CGM) around Milky Way-mass (MW-mass) galaxies is critical to a full understanding of galaxy evolution. In this second paper of the "X-rays in Romulus25" series, we unpack the specific physical processes giving rise to the presence of hot X-ray emitting gas in the halos of galaxies from the Romulus25 (R25) simulation, focusing on L$_{*}$ galaxies. We determine that a strong correlation appears between the mass of hot CGM gas, M$_{gas, T > 10^{5.5} K}$, and the X-ray emissivity, $ε_χ$, measured in the first paper of this series, (Sanchez et al. 2026a, submitted). There is also a secondary correlation between M$_{gas, T > 10^{5.5} K}$ and $ε_χ$ with the average metallicity of the hot CGM gas, $\bar{Z}_{gas, T > 10^{5.5} K}$. We use the well-studied PIONEER simulations from Sanchez et al. (2019), a set of zoom-in MW-mass galaxies run with the genetic modification technique of Roth et al. (2016) and the same physics as R25, to interpret these correlations. We determine that the presence of hot X-ray emitting gas is determined by two key processes: 1) the quantity of hot gas mass in the CGM, M$_{gas, T > 10^{5.5} K}$, is set by the combined total energy injection of $both$ stellar and AGN feedback, and 2) together the average temperature and metallicity of the hot CGM changes the soft X-ray spectrum of the gas resulting in brighter metal-rich CGM and dimmer metal-poor CGM for the same quantity of M$_{gas, T > 10^{5.5} K}$. These results indicate, for the first time, that metal-rich gas halos may bias X-ray observations of MW-mass galaxies.

title: Resolving the thermal component of stellar feedback with the "anchor-and-refine" scheme in galactic simulations
comment: 11 pages and 8 figs in the main text; A&A in press
summary: (abridged) Stellar feedback regulates galactic baryon cycles, but galaxy-scale simulations often cannot resolve supernova cooling radii. Momentum-based subgrid models can consequently underresolve the hot gas around young stars. We develop an "anchor-and-refine" feedback scheme that anchors a host cell near each star particle, preventing its displacement and preserving a thermal-feedback reservoir. When the cooling radius is resolved, all supernova energy is injected into the host cell as thermal energy; otherwise, the host cell is refined and terminal momentum is deposited into surrounding gas cells. Idealized tests agree with high-resolution simulations, yielding consistent superbubble properties and preserving hot interiors without artificial cooling. In an isolated Milky Way-mass galaxy, the scheme captures finer X-ray-emitting structures and a sharply defined, X-ray-bright central mid-plane. It also produces a smoother star formation history than pure hybrid feedback. Hot gas dominates outflow mass loading, with the mass-loading factor plateauing at approximately 0.2 at heights z>1 kpc. Phase decomposition indicates that hot gas sustains a steady, energy-driven wind, whereas cooler outflows decline with height because of radiative cooling and gravitational fallback. These results highlight the role of thermal feedback in driving galactic winds. By preserving hot superbubble interiors and the partition of thermal and kinetic energy, anchor-and-refine improves the treatment of hot gas, star formation, and feedback at limited resolution, supporting future applications to galaxy-scale and cosmological zoom-in simulations.

title: Circular Axion String Loop Simulations: Field Theory and Effective Description
comment: Main part: 48 pages, 18 figures. Appendices: 28 pages, 9 additional figures. Comments welcome!
summary: An accurate description of axion strings and their radiation is crucial for understanding their cosmological implications. Motivated by the differing conclusions of previous works, we study a simple, controlled setup: the collapse of an initially static circular loop in a Minkowski background. We compare field-theory simulations of the conventional complex scalar and high-tension Klaer--Moore models with solutions of the renormalised Nambu--Goto--Kalb--Ramond (NGKR) equation of motion, covering the range $3 \lesssim \mathcal{T} \lesssim 100$ in dimensionless string tension. Both the field theory and NGKR approach the Nambu--Goto (NG) limit with corrections scaling as $1/\mathcal{T}$. However, the leading correction to the halving-time is $20-35\%$ larger in NGKR than in the field-theory simulations over the same range of tensions, while for large tensions the value agrees with an independent perturbative calculation to $0.2\%$. The late-time axion spectrum agrees with NGKR in the infrared, but the collapse generates additional structure in the ultraviolet part of the spectrum, which we attribute to different events such as an outgoing wave front that carries a sizable fraction of the energy or the rebound of the initial loop. These results provide a useful benchmark for a more accurate understanding of axion radiation from cosmological string networks.

title: Hot off the Stacks: X-rays in Romulus25, Part I - Comparisons to Observations from eRosita
comment: 13 pages, 6 figures, submitted to The Astrophysical Journal
summary: Recent observations from the from Spectrum Roentgen Gamma (SRG)/eROSITA all-sky survey data have helped to illuminate the hot circumgalactic medium (CGM) around galaxies at Milky Way-masses and above. In our study, we explore the hot X-ray emitting (T \textgreater 10$^6$ K) component of the CGM in over 750 galaxies from the Romulus25 cosmological simulation (Tremmel et al. 2017) between 10.0 < log(M$_*/M_{\odot}$) < 11.5. We forward-model soft X-ray [0.5 - 2.0] keV observations of our simulated galaxies using pyXSIM and SIXTE to measure the X-ray surface brightness (SB) profiles of the hot CGM. We then compare the average X-ray surface brightness profiles of six stellar-mass selected sub-samples to compare to the observational results from Chadayammuri et al. (2022a) and Zhang et al. 2024a. Broadly, we find that our stacked SB profiles are too bright compared to observations from Chadayammuri et al. (2022a) and Zhang et al.(2024a) particularly in the inner CGM. Additionally, we calculate the X-ray luminosity (L$_χ$) of the hot CGM for each galaxy and compare the average L$_χ$ across stellar mass to observations from Zhang et al. (2024b) as well as measurements from the EAGLE, TNG, SIMBA simulations. Across stellar mass, the average L$_χ$ of galaxies from Romulus25 are brighter than observations except at the lower, Milky Way-mass end where we are in relative agreement with both observations and most other simulations. We also consider a zero-metallicity emission model, because Romulus25 does not have metal-line cooling, finding the average L$_χ$ decreases by nearly an order-of-magnitude, which better matches observations particularly in the Milky Way-mass regime.

title: Seeing Unseen Gravitational Wave Inspirals at the Galactic Center
comment: Accepted for publication ApJ Letters
summary: The Galactic Center is expected to host a population of extremely large mass-ratio inspirals (X-MRIs) migrating toward the supermassive black hole. We propose an observational approach utilizing the secular gravitational torque exerted by X-MRIs on the highly eccentric S-star S301. This approach is intrinsically limited by the stochastic nature of the surrounding stellar-mass black hole cusp. As S301 propagates through this granular medium, it experiences discrete gravitational encounters. Standard orbital fitting procedures inherently assume a smooth background potential; applying them to stochastic trajectories averages these discrete velocity discontinuities into a continuous secular drift. This introduces a systematic bias that mimics the X-MRI precession signal, invalidating traditional mass estimation techniques. To resolve this degeneracy, we implement a methodology based on the Wavelet Transform Modulus Maxima method to characterize the local Hölder regularity of the orbital motion. This model isolates the singular discontinuities induced by stellar-mass black hole encounters from the continuous torque of the X-MRI distribution, allowing for detection even when instantaneous accelerations are below the instrumental noise threshold. We demonstrate analytically that S301 is highly sensitive to the interior X-MRI population while remaining dynamically decoupled from the secular influence of the exterior cusp. Combining precision astrometry and radial velocity projections, we establish that a minimal population of two X-MRIs is detectable within a five to nine-year timeframe, allowing us to constrain the presence of an unseen orbiter population prior to the launch of space-based gravitational wave detectors.
